claim: COVID-19 vaccination averted an estimated 14.4M (official-death basis) to 19.8M (excess-mortality basis) deaths globally in the first year of rollout (8 Dec 2020 - 8 Dec 2021), across 185 countries/territories.
source_title: Global impact of the first year of COVID-19 vaccination: a mathematical modelling study
authors: Watson OJ, Barnsley G, Toor J, Hogan AB, Winskill P, Ghani AC
trust_tier: Tier 1 - peer-reviewed, but a MODELLING study, not a direct observational count
exact_quote_or_stat: 19.8 million deaths averted (of a possible 31.4 million) using excess-mortality-based fitting; 14.4 million deaths averted using official reported COVID-19 death counts. Published Lancet Infect Dis 2022; 22: 1293-1302 (print issue Sept 2022, online 23 June 2022). 79% (15.5M) of averted deaths attributed to direct vaccine protection, 21% (4.3M) to indirect effects (reduced transmission/healthcare burden). Regional: ~7.5 million deaths averted in COVAX-covered countries; modelling suggests up to ~1.5M more deaths (599,300 + 81,750 figures reported by Imperial College press materials) could have been averted had COVAX/WHO coverage targets been met. China excluded from the analysis 'due to its unique position as the origin of the detected epidemic and its large influence on estimates.'
notes: This is a COUNTERFACTUAL MATHEMATICAL MODEL (compares actual outcomes to a simulated 'no vaccine' scenario), not a direct causal/observational tally - this is the paper's own framing, not an external caveat. A correction notice was also published by the Lancet (PIIS1473-3099(23)00566-2) - should be checked if reproducing exact figures in a notebook, as it may adjust minor details. A non-peer-reviewed preprint critique (Rancourt & Hickey, Authorea, 'Quantitative evaluation of whether the Nobel-Prize-winning COVID-19 vaccine actually saved millions of lives') argues the model's assumptions are 'highly improbable' - documented below as NOT a credible peer-reviewed counter-source (see counter-evidence entries).

claim: The May 2024 BMJ Public Health paper claiming >3 million excess deaths across 47 Western countries, later used to imply a vaccine-mortality link, was retracted in August 2026.
source_title: RETRACTED: Excess mortality across countries in the Western World since the COVID-19 pandemic: 'Our World in Data' estimates of January 2020 to December 2022
authors: Mostert S, Hoogland M, Huibers M, Kaspers G
doi_or_url: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjph-2023-000282 (original article DOI, now shows RETRACTED prefix); retraction notice at bmjpublichealth.bmj.com/content/4/3/e000282ret
trust_tier: Tier 1 (meta) - official journal retraction notice; original paper's causal framing was found unsound
exact_quote_or_stat: Original paper (BMJ Public Health 2024;2:e000282, published 6 May 2024) reported total excess deaths of 3,098,456 across 47 Western-world countries from 1 Jan 2020 to 31 Dec 2022 (1,033,122 in 2020; 1,256,942 in 2021; 808,392 in 2022). Expression of Concern (DOI 10.1136/bmjph-2023-000282eoc, published 14 June 2024) stated: the paper's authors 'looked only at trends in excess mortality over time, not its causes' and the study 'does not support the claim that vaccines are a major contributory factor to excess deaths since the start of the pandemic' - i.e. the paper ITSELF, even before retraction, did not establish the causal vaccine link that was attributed to it in public discourse. Retraction notice (11 Aug 2026) reason: 'misinformation in the discussion regarding the possible causes of excess mortality, and because the limited nature of the original work by the authors was not sufficiently described.' Investigation conducted by the Princess Maxima Center (Netherlands, institution of 3 of 4 authors). Co-authors Kaspers and Huibers supported the retraction; corresponding author Mostert and co-author Hoogland disagreed with it.
notes: IMPORTANT PRECISION FIX vs prior summary: (1) original publication date is 6 May 2024 (prior summary said 'May 2024' - correct), but note some outlets list the DOI-visible journal year/volume as 2024;2:e000282 with a retraction record appearing at 4/3/e000282ret in 2026 (BMJ's continuous-volume numbering can look inconsistent across mirrors - use the DOI as the canonical identifier). (2) Exact headline number is 3,098,456 (not merely '>3 million' - use the precise figure). (3) Timeline: expression of concern in June 2024 (triggered by a public retraction request from demographer Ariel Karlinsky), Mostert testified before a US Senate subcommittee 3 June 2026, retraction followed ~2 months later (11 Aug 2026). (4) The investigating committee found NO scientific misconduct or malicious intent - attributed the problems to carelessness, gaps in knowledge, and negligence, not fraud. This nuance should be preserved in the notebook rather than implying deliberate fraud.

claim: A peer-reviewed (non-retracted, non-preprint) paper published in a legitimate journal found a HIGHER rate of serious adverse events of special interest in mRNA-vaccinated randomized trial participants than in placebo recipients - the strongest credible counter-evidence located in this search.
source_title: Serious adverse events of special interest following mRNA COVID-19 vaccination in randomized trials in adults
authors: Fraiman J, Erviti J, Jones M, Greenland S, Whelan P, Kaplan RM, Doshi P
trust_tier: Tier 1 (formally peer-reviewed, published, NOT retracted) - but with SUBSTANTIVE, SPECIFIC methodological critiques published by other scientists (see notes); include with both sides stated
exact_quote_or_stat: Secondary reanalysis of the Pfizer (NCT04368728) and Moderna (NCT04470427) phase III placebo-controlled RCT data, using an adapted Brighton Collaboration list of 'adverse events of special interest.' Found an excess risk of serious adverse events of special interest of 10.1 per 10,000 vaccinated (Pfizer) and 15.1 per 10,000 vaccinated (Moderna), against reported placebo-arm baseline rates of 17.6 and 42.2 per 10,000 respectively (i.e., the excess figures represent the vaccine-minus-placebo difference in serious-AESI rates, not the absolute rate).
notes: THIS IS EXACTLY THE KIND OF SOURCE ITEM 6 ASKED FOR - a real, peer-reviewed, non-retracted paper in a mainstream Elsevier journal that reports a vaccine-arm excess of serious adverse events, and it should be included and NOT dismissed. However, fairness requires noting the substantive, specific published criticism it has received: critics (writing in Science-Based Medicine, a science-communication outlet, not itself a peer-reviewed rebuttal) argued the paper (a) compared TOTAL ADVERSE EVENT COUNTS rather than counts of AFFECTED PARTICIPANTS, inflating vaccine-arm totals when one person had multiple related events; (b) applied event-category inclusion/exclusion inconsistently (e.g. diarrhea included, vomiting excluded); (c) compared adverse-event rates against COVID-19 hospitalization rates, which critics call a mismatched comparison. The journal Vaccine reportedly published two critical commentaries (2023, 2024) about the paper; the original authors submitted a response letter in Jan 2025 that the editor-in-chief reportedly rejected without peer review (per secondary reporting, not independently verified with the original correspondence). Present this as: a real, legitimately-published, non-retracted finding of excess serious-AE risk in trial data, WITH documented, specific methodological objections from other researchers - let the reader see both, rather than either uncritically citing it or dismissing it outright.
